Boy bands.Boyzone: The Irish band, led by Ronan Keating, was formed in 1993, and Love Me for a Reason was an early hit.
Boy bands.BTS: The group became the first Korean act to top the US Billboard Hot 100 with Dynamite in 2020, and their fan base is called the ARMY.
Boy bands.Boyz II Men: Their End of the Road spent 13 weeks at number one in 1992, a record at the time.
Boy bands.New Edition: The Boston group formed in 1978, and spawned Bell Biv DeVoe and launched Bobby Brown.
Boy bands.Menudo: The Puerto Rican group, from 1977, famously replaced members when they turned 16, and launched Ricky Martin.
Boy bands.Spice Girls: A trap. This is a girl group, with Wannabe topping charts in the 1990s.
Boy bands.Destiny's Child: A girl group, with Beyonce as lead singer, and Survivor a favourite.
Boy bands.Little Mix: The girl group won The X Factor in 2011, the first group to win it.
Boy bands.Coldplay: A rock band, famous for Yellow and Fix You, not a boy band.
Boy bands.Metallica: A heavy metal band, famous for Enter Sandman, not a boy band.
Boy bands.Oasis: A British guitar band from Manchester, led by the Gallagher brothers, who played rock, not boy band pop.
Boy bands.Girls Aloud: A girl group put together on the TV show Popstars: The Rivals in 2002.
Boy bands.The Supremes: A Motown girl group with Diana Ross, whose hits like Baby Love topped charts.
Boy bands.Maroon 5: A trap. All male, but Maroon 5 is a pop-rock band that plays its own instruments, which is not the boy band formula.
Boy bands.Bon Jovi: A trap. Bon Jovi is all male, but a rock band that plays instruments.
Boy bands.ABBA: The Swedish group had two men and two women, so it is not a boy band.
Boy bands.Fleetwood Mac: A mixed band of men and women, famous for Rumours, one of the best-selling albums ever.
Boy bands.The Bangles: A girl group from California, with Walk Like an Egyptian and Eternal Flame as hits.
Boy bands.TLC: A girl trio with nicknames like T-Boz and Left Eye, famous for Waterfalls.

Video game characters who are animals.Sonic: Sega's hedgehog moves at supersonic speeds; designer Naoto Ohshima's blue colour matched Sega's logo.
Video game characters who are animals.Tails: Sonic's sidekick is a fox with two tails, which he can spin to fly like a helicopter; his real name is Miles Prower, a pun on 'miles per hour'.
Video game characters who are animals.Knuckles: An echidna, a spiny egg-laying Australian mammal, that guards the Master Emerald; his first appearance was in Sonic 3 (1994).
Video game characters who are animals.Crash Bandicoot: A bandicoot is a small marsupial from Australia, and Crash was created by Naughty Dog for the first PlayStation.
Video game characters who are animals.Spyro: A small purple dragon, so he counts as a mythical animal; his 1998 debut was a platformer hit on PlayStation.
Video game characters who are animals.Donkey Kong: A gorilla who started as the villain of the 1981 arcade game; his son-turned-hero version came later.
Video game characters who are animals.Diddy Kong: A chimp and Donkey Kong's sidekick, he first appeared in Donkey Kong Country on the SNES in 1994.
Video game characters who are animals.Fox McCloud: Star Fox's pilot, a fox who leads a team of anthropomorphic animals, with a father named James.
Video game characters who are animals.Yoshi: A dinosaur of sorts, whose tongue can extend to swallow enemies; he debuted in Super Mario World in 1990.
Video game characters who are animals.Banjo: A honey bear, partnered with a breegull named Kazooie who lives in his backpack; the duo are from Rare's 1998 platformer.
Video game characters who are animals.Kazooie: A red breegull, a species invented by Rare, who lives in Banjo's backpack and can fire eggs.
Video game characters who are animals.Sly Cooper: A raccoon master thief whose family cane hides his tools; the series was created by Sucker Punch for PlayStation 2.
Video game characters who are animals.Mario: A trap: Mario is a human plumber, not an animal, even though he wears a raccoon or tanooki suit in some games.
Video game characters who are animals.Luigi: Mario's brother is human; like Mario, he wears animal-themed power-ups but isn't one himself.
Video game characters who are animals.Link: The hero of Zelda is a Hylian, an elf-eared human, not an animal; the princess is Zelda, which is why people confuse the names.
Video game characters who are animals.Zelda: The princess of Hyrule is a Hylian, who is human-like, and not the hero of her own game series until recently.
Video game characters who are animals.Lara Croft: A British archaeologist in Tomb Raider, who is human, though she fights plenty of animals along the way.
Video game characters who are animals.Master Chief: A genetically enhanced human supersoldier in armor, so no animal there, in Halo.
Video game characters who are animals.Pac-Man: A round yellow creature with a mouth, not a real animal; his ghosts are Blinky, Pinky, Inky and Clyde.
Video game characters who are animals.Kirby: A pink puffball is a creature of its own invention; he isn't any animal, even though he inhales enemies.
Video game characters who are animals.Samus: A human bounty hunter in power armor, whose gender was a twist in 1986's Metroid.
Video game characters who are animals.Mega Man: A blue android created by Dr. Light, so a robot, not an animal; his dog Rush is though.
Video game characters who are animals.Kratos: The Spartan hero of God of War is a demigod and so a human, not an animal.
Video game characters who are animals.Steve: Minecraft's default skin is a human, not an animal, though there are pigs and cows all around in the game.

Sports done on horseback.Polo: Sometimes called 'the sport of kings', it's played on a pitch about ten football fields in size, with riders switching ponies between chukkas.
Sports done on horseback.Show jumping: Riders must clear a course of fences without knocking them down, and faults come from poles dropped or refusals.
Sports done on horseback.Dressage: Riders guide horses through precise movements with almost invisible aids, and the sport's origin goes back to ancient Greece and military training.
Sports done on horseback.Horse racing: Every Thoroughbred in the world descends from just three Arabian stallions, the Byerley Turk, Darley Arabian and Godolphin Arabian.
Sports done on horseback.Barrel racing: Mostly a rodeo event for women, in which horse and rider run a cloverleaf pattern around three barrels.
Sports done on horseback.Eventing: A three-part equestrian event of dressage, cross-country and show jumping, once called 'the military'.
Sports done on horseback.Buzkashi: Afghanistan's national sport, where mounted players fight to carry a goat or calf carcass to a scoring circle.
Sports done on horseback.Tent pegging: Riders gallop and use a lance or sword to pick up a small peg from the ground; it comes from cavalry training.
Sports done on horseback.Polocrosse: A mix of polo and lacrosse invented in Australia in the 1930s, played with one horse and a racquet with a net.
Sports done on horseback.Horseball: A French invention like basketball on horseback, with players passing a ball with handles into a hoop.
Sports done on horseback.Jousting: Medieval knights charged each other with lances, and it is the official sport of the US state of Maryland.
Sports done on horseback.Water polo: Played in a pool, with no horses; a trap, since 'polo' is also played on horseback.
Sports done on horseback.Pommel horse: A gymnastics apparatus shaped like a horse but not a real one.
Sports done on horseback.Croquet: Played on foot with mallets on a lawn, and not on horseback.
Sports done on horseback.Bowls: A lawn sport played on foot, with weighted balls aimed at a small jack.
Sports done on horseback.Curling: On ice with stones, which can't be done on horseback.
Sports done on horseback.Camel racing: A popular sport in Arabian countries, with camels instead of horses; some use robot jockeys.
Sports done on horseback.Bull riding: A rodeo event in which cowboys ride bucking bulls, not horses.
Sports done on horseback.Greyhound racing: Dogs race after a mechanical lure and no riders are involved.
Sports done on horseback.Sled dog racing: Dogs pulling a sled, such as the Iditarod in Alaska, are involved in place of horses.
Sports done on horseback.Motocross: Motorcycles race over rough dirt tracks, no horses involved.
Sports done on horseback.Cycling: A rider and bike, with 'horsepower' not coming from a real horse.
Sports done on horseback.Rowing: Powered by oars on water, no horses involved.
Sports done on horseback.Canoeing: Paddling on water, with no horse involved.

English football clubs.Arsenal: Founded by munitions workers in southeast London in 1886, as Dial Square; the club still has a cannon on its badge.
English football clubs.Chelsea: Based in Fulham, not Chelsea, because the club was named after the borough that wouldn't host the team; it won the Champions League in 2012 and 2021.
English football clubs.Liverpool: Founded in 1892, after Everton left Anfield, and its anthem 'You'll Never Walk Alone' is sung before each home game.
English football clubs.Everton: The first club to play at Anfield, they're one of the founding members of the Football League in 1888.
English football clubs.Tottenham: Called Spurs, they became the first 20th century club to win the league and FA Cup double in 1961.
English football clubs.Manchester United: The team started as Newton Heath, a railway workers' side, and lost eight players in the 1958 Munich air disaster.
English football clubs.Aston Villa: Won the European Cup in 1982, one of only a handful of English clubs ever to do so.
English football clubs.Newcastle United: Known as the Magpies for their black-and-white stripes, they play at St James' Park.
English football clubs.Leeds United: Formed in 1919, they won the First Division in 1992, and were renowned for their 'Dirty Leeds' reputation in the 1970s.
English football clubs.West Ham: Called 'The Hammers' because the club began as a works team of the Thames Ironworks.
English football clubs.Fulham: London's oldest professional club, founded in 1879, and plays at Craven Cottage by the Thames.
English football clubs.Brentford: A west London club that returned to the Premier League in 2021 after 74 years.
English football clubs.Barcelona: A Spanish club from Catalonia, whose motto is 'more than a club'.
English football clubs.Real Madrid: A Spanish club with a record 15 European Cup and Champions League titles.
English football clubs.Juventus: An Italian club from Turin, nicknamed 'the Old Lady'.
English football clubs.Ajax: A Dutch club from Amsterdam, which pioneered 'Total Football' under Rinus Michels and Johan Cruyff.
English football clubs.Celtic: A Scottish club from Glasgow that won the European Cup in 1967, the first British club to do so.
English football clubs.Rangers: Celtic's Old Firm rival in Glasgow, a Scottish club, so they're not in England.
English football clubs.Bayern Munich: A German club with the most Bundesliga titles, which is not in England.
English football clubs.PSG: A Paris club, founded in 1970, which is a French club.
English football clubs.Benfica: A Portuguese club from Lisbon, with an eagle as its mascot, who flies around the pitch before home games.
English football clubs.Porto: A Portuguese club from the north, which won the Champions League in 2004 under Jose Mourinho.
English football clubs.Inter Milan: An Italian club founded in 1908 for being international, as it admitted foreign players.
English football clubs.Galatasaray: A Turkish club from Istanbul, whose fans' loud atmosphere gave its stadium the nickname 'Hell'.

Sports where players wear skates.Ice hockey: Players can reach about 30 km/h on skates, and the sport has been on the Olympic program since 1920.
Sports where players wear skates.Roller derby: Teams of five race around an oval track on quad skates, with jammers scoring by passing opponents.
Sports where players wear skates.Speed skating: Racers on long blades can top 50 km/h, and the clap skate's hinged blade added speed after 1997.
Sports where players wear skates.Figure skating: Triple and quadruple jumps involve spinning in the air at about 300 rpm, and a quad jump was first landed in competition in 1988.
Sports where players wear skates.Bandy: Played on ice with skates and a ball, it's one of the world's biggest winter sports in Russia and Sweden.
Sports where players wear skates.Ringette: Players skate and pass a rubber ring with straight sticks, and it was invented in Canada in the 1960s.
Sports where players wear skates.Inline hockey: Players on inline skates play on a hard floor and use a puck or a ball, and it's like hockey without ice.
Sports where players wear skates.Roller hockey: Players on quad skates play hockey on a hard surface, and it's a sport with long traditions in Spain and Portugal.
Sports where players wear skates.Short track: Skaters race in packs round a small oval of about 111 meters, and crashes and passing moves are a big part of the action.
Sports where players wear skates.Ice dancing: Couples perform to music on the ice, and it joined the Olympics in 1976 as a sport.
Sports where players wear skates.Synchronized skating: Teams of 8 to 20 skaters perform together in formation, and it's one of the sport's fastest-growing disciplines.
Sports where players wear skates.Curling: Players wear shoes with a slider on one foot, not skates, so they can glide as they deliver the stone.
Sports where players wear skates.Broomball: Players wear shoes with grippy soles on ice and use a broom-like stick to hit a ball, so no skates.
Sports where players wear skates.Luge: Riders lie on their backs on a sled, going feet first at speeds that can top 130 km/h, and the runners are steel blades, not skates.
Sports where players wear skates.Skeleton: Riders slide headfirst on a small sled down an ice track, and no skates are involved.
Sports where players wear skates.Bobsleigh: A team rides a steel sled down an ice track, and the brakeman pushes at the start.
Sports where players wear skates.Skateboarding: It uses a wheeled board, and the sport debuted at the Olympics in 2020 in Tokyo, but players don't wear skates.
Sports where players wear skates.Snowboarding: Riders strap onto a single board, not skates, and the sport entered the Olympics in 1998.
Sports where players wear skates.Alpine skiing: Skiers glide on skis, not skates, and downhill racers can top 130 km/h.
Sports where players wear skates.Ski jumping: Athletes fly more than 200 meters on skis, and they get no skates.
Sports where players wear skates.Biathlon: It combines cross-country skiing with rifle shooting, and athletes wear skis.
Sports where players wear skates.Field hockey: Players wear cleats on grass or turf, with no skates, and the sticks are used to hit a ball.
Sports where players wear skates.Floorball: Players run on an indoor court in sneakers, not skates, and the sport began in Scandinavia.
Sports where players wear skates.Lacrosse: Players wear cleats and run on a field, so no skates, though box lacrosse is played in an arena.

Famous cricketers.Sachin Tendulkar: India's Little Master scored 100 international centuries, a record no one else is close to, and played for 24 years from age 16.
Famous cricketers.Don Bradman: His Test average of 99.94 is the most famous number in cricket; needing just four runs in his last innings, he was dismissed for a duck.
Famous cricketers.Shane Warne: His first ball in an Ashes Test in 1993 curved so far it was called the Ball of the Century. He took 708 Test wickets, mostly with leg spin.
Famous cricketers.Virat Kohli: The Indian batter has scored more than 80 international centuries and is celebrated for his chasing of big totals in one-day games.
Famous cricketers.Brian Lara: The West Indian left-hander holds the Test record of 400 not out, made in 2004, and once scored 501 in a single first-class innings.
Famous cricketers.Ian Botham: England's all-rounder starred in the 1981 Ashes, nicknamed Beefy, and later raised millions by walking the length of Britain for charity.
Famous cricketers.Viv Richards: The Antiguan once hit the fastest Test century in 56 balls, in 1986, and he famously never wore a helmet against the fastest bowlers.
Famous cricketers.Jacques Kallis: South Africa's all-rounder scored over 13,000 Test runs and also took about 290 wickets, a combination matched by almost no one.
Famous cricketers.MS Dhoni: India's captain won the T20 World Cup, the 50-over World Cup and the Champions Trophy, and is nicknamed Captain Cool for his calm.
Famous cricketers.Muttiah Muralitharan: Sri Lanka's off-spinner took 800 Test wickets, the most ever, using unusually flexible wrists to turn the ball sharply.
Famous cricketers.Ricky Ponting: Australia's captain won two World Cups in a row as skipper, in 2003 and 2007, and scored over 13,000 Test runs.
Famous cricketers.Joe Root: England's batter passed 12,000 Test runs and has more Test centuries than any other England player, often playing with calm in a crisis.
Famous cricketers.Babe Ruth: The baseball slugger hit 714 home runs, and more than that, once out-homered whole teams in a season. He has no place in a cricket game.
Famous cricketers.Derek Jeter: A New York Yankees shortstop with five World Series wins, his stage was baseball, not cricket, even if his bat-and-ball sport is a distant cousin.
Famous cricketers.Wayne Rooney: England's record scorer for years and Manchester United's all-time top scorer, he played football rather than cricket.
Famous cricketers.David Beckham: Famous for his curling free kicks for England and Manchester United, he was a footballer; the bend in the ball is the only link to spin bowling.
Famous cricketers.Jonny Wilkinson: The rugby fly-half kicked the drop goal that won England the 2003 World Cup in extra time. Rugby, not cricket.
Famous cricketers.Andy Murray: The Scottish tennis player won Wimbledon in 2013, ending a 77-year wait for a British men's champion. Tennis, not cricket.
Famous cricketers.Usain Bolt: The sprinter holds the 100 metres record of 9.58 seconds. He loved cricket as a boy in Jamaica, but became a runner, not a batter.
Famous cricketers.Roger Federer: The Swiss tennis player won 20 Grand Slam singles titles, and gets lumped in with cricket gentlemen only by his white Wimbledon outfit.
Famous cricketers.Rory McIlroy: The Northern Irish golfer has won four major championships. Golf shares cricket's etiquette but not its ball or bat.
Famous cricketers.Mo Farah: The British distance runner won both the 5,000 and 10,000 metres at two straight Olympics, 2012 and 2016.
Famous cricketers.Jonah Lomu: The New Zealand rugby wing became a global star at the 1995 World Cup, bowling over defenders at 120 kilograms.
Famous cricketers.Lewis Hamilton: The British driver has won seven Formula 1 world titles, tying Michael Schumacher. He drives cars, not cricket balls.

Ancient Greeks (any field).Pericles: He led Athens at the height of its power in the 400s BC, and the Parthenon was built under his leadership.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Homer: The Iliad and Odyssey are credited to him, but whether one person composed both has been debated for centuries.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Herodotus: Called the Father of History. His Histories tell of the Persian Wars, with plenty of tall tales along the way.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Archimedes: The mathematician of Syracuse found the principle of buoyancy, and a Roman soldier killed him in 212 BC.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Euclid: His Elements, a geometry textbook, was used for over 2,000 years.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Hippocrates: Called the father of medicine, he pushed for natural causes of disease. The medical oath is attributed to his school.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Sophocles: He wrote Oedipus Rex and Antigone, and won many drama contests in Athens.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Leonidas: The Spartan king held Thermopylae in 480 BC against the Persians, with his 300 Spartans and thousands of allies.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Sappho: A poet of Lesbos, so admired she was called the tenth Muse. Only fragments of her work survive.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Aesop: The fables' teller, possibly once enslaved, gave us the Tortoise and the Hare.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Aristophanes: A comic playwright whose Lysistrata imagines women ending a war by refusing to sleep with their husbands.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Solon: An Athenian lawgiver who cancelled many debts in about 594 BC, paving the way for democracy.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Julius Caesar: A Roman general and dictator, not a Greek. He did speak Greek and quoted it as he died, according to legend.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Cicero: Rome's greatest orator, who studied in Greece but was a Roman.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Nero: A Roman emperor who loved Greek culture. He even competed in the Greek Olympics, but was Roman.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Confucius: The Chinese thinker taught around the same period as Socrates, but far to the east.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Hannibal: A Carthaginian general from North Africa, who crossed the Alps with elephants.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Ramses II: An Egyptian pharaoh who reigned for 66 years, about 700 years before the Parthenon.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Virgil: A Roman poet who wrote the Aeneid. He borrowed Greek models but was Roman.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Ovid: A Roman poet who wrote Metamorphoses, retelling Greek myths from a Roman viewpoint.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Spartacus: A Thracian gladiator who led a slave revolt against Rome in 73 BC. He was Thracian, not Greek.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Attila: King of the Huns in the 400s AD, centuries after ancient Greece's golden age.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Boudica: A British queen who rebelled against Rome in AD 60 or 61. Nothing Greek.
Ancient Greeks (any field).Xerxes: The Persian king who invaded Greece in 480 BC. He was the Greeks' enemy, not one of them.

Household things that need water to work.Washing machine: A typical machine uses roughly 15 to 40 gallons of water per load, with newer front-loaders at the lower end.
Household things that need water to work.Dishwasher: A modern dishwasher can use less water than washing the same dishes by hand, especially if you skip pre-rinsing.
Household things that need water to work.Kettle: Electric kettles boil water quickly with a heating element at the base, and they shut off by sensing steam.
Household things that need water to work.Coffee maker: A drip machine heats water to just under boiling with a simple pump-like effect, forcing it up and over the grounds.
Household things that need water to work.Steam iron: The steam comes from water heated in the soleplate, and using distilled water helps avoid limescale clogging its vents.
Household things that need water to work.Shower: Showerheads sold in the US are usually capped by law at about 2.5 gallons a minute.
Household things that need water to work.Toilet: A flush tank uses gravity: water rushing down creates a siphon that pulls waste through the bend in the trap.
Household things that need water to work.Humidifier: Ultrasonic humidifiers make a cool mist with a vibrating plate, and tap water minerals can leave a fine white dust.
Household things that need water to work.Garden hose: Garden hoses are often color-coded and labeled, and a regular one is not safe for drinking unless marked as drinking-water safe.
Household things that need water to work.Sprinkler: The impact sprinkler's rhythmic tick-tick comes from a spring-loaded arm that is knocked by the water jet, which makes it rotate.
Household things that need water to work.Ice maker: A home ice maker fills a tray from a water line, freezes it, and then warms the tray slightly so the cubes drop out.
Household things that need water to work.Pressure washer: Pressure washers blast water at pressures often over 1,500 psi, enough to strip paint or damage wood if misused.
Household things that need water to work.Water pistol: Squirt guns rely on a simple pump or trigger piston, and the Super Soaker was invented by NASA engineer Lonnie Johnson.
Household things that need water to work.Toaster: It needs only electricity. A toaster's glowing wires run at roughly 1,000 degrees, and water inside is a shock hazard, not a feature.
Household things that need water to work.Hair dryer: It needs air and electricity, with no water involved, and a fan pulls room air across a heated coil.
Household things that need water to work.Lamp: A lamp needs only power. Water and light bulbs mix badly, which is why bathroom fixtures carry special wet ratings.
Household things that need water to work.Television: It needs only electricity and signal. A TV left outdoors in the rain is a strong lesson in how little water electronics tolerate.
Household things that need water to work.Desk fan: It only needs a motor and power, but many fans can spritz a mist; a plain one does not need any water.
Household things that need water to work.Radio: It needs power and a signal, nothing wet. Early crystal radios needed no battery, drawing energy from the radio waves themselves.
Household things that need water to work.Stapler: It runs on your hand alone, with a spring and a bit of metal bending, and it needs no water or power.
Household things that need water to work.Air fryer: It cooks with hot circulating air, not water or oil, so it is in effect a small, powerful convection oven.
Household things that need water to work.Doorbell: A doorbell needs only a small electrical circuit or battery, not water, though some smart ones can run in the rain.
Household things that need water to work.Calculator: Solar-powered calculators run on light alone, which makes them a classic example of an appliance that needs no water.
Household things that need water to work.Paper shredder: It runs on electricity alone. Cross-cut shredders turn a page into confetti-size bits that are very hard to piece back together.

Types of bag.Backpack: Backpacks spread weight over both shoulders, and doctors suggest carrying no more than about 10 to 15 percent of body weight.
Types of bag.Tote bag: A tote bag is an open carry-all, and the word 'tote' dates to the 1600s, meaning to carry or haul.
Types of bag.Duffel bag: The duffel is named for Duffel, a Belgian town that made the thick woolen cloth once used for these bags.
Types of bag.Briefcase: A briefcase is a flat, hard-sided case for papers, and the name comes from legal 'briefs' that lawyers carried in them.
Types of bag.Handbag: The handbag hangs from the arm or hand, and it's called a purse in the US, where a purse in Britain means a wallet.
Types of bag.Clutch: A clutch has no strap and is held in the hand, and it's a favorite for evening wear, as it holds only the essentials.
Types of bag.Satchel: A satchel is a bag with a shoulder strap and flap, long used by schoolchildren, and the word goes back to the Latin for sack.
Types of bag.Messenger bag: Messenger bags were made for bike couriers, and the single cross-body strap lets you swing the bag around to the front.
Types of bag.Fanny pack: A fanny pack is a belt bag, and in Britain 'fanny' has a different meaning, so there it's called a bum bag.
Types of bag.Grocery bag: The flat-bottomed paper grocery bag was invented in 1871 by Margaret Knight, who also held dozens of other patents.
Types of bag.Garment bag: A garment bag lets you carry suits and dresses folded or hanging, and many fit into overhead airplane compartments.
Types of bag.Diaper bag: A diaper bag is a parent's mobile base, and it's usually bigger than a normal tote, with many pockets for supplies.
Types of bag.Cardboard box: A cardboard box is a container but not a bag, and corrugated board was patented in 1856, first for hat linings.
Types of bag.Basket: A basket is woven from reeds or similar materials, and it's one of the oldest human crafts, going back over 10,000 years.
Types of bag.Crate: A crate is a rigid wooden or plastic container, so it's a box rather than a flexible bag.
Types of bag.Bucket: A bucket is a rigid container with a handle, so it's not a bag, even though some buckets have lids.
Types of bag.Barrel: A barrel is a wooden cask, and it's the traditional way of aging wine and whiskey, but it isn't a bag.
Types of bag.Jar: A jar is a rigid container made of glass or plastic, which is quite different from a flexible bag.
Types of bag.Drawer: A drawer slides in and out of furniture; it holds things, but it is built into something and isn't carried like a bag.
Types of bag.Tray: A tray is flat with a rim, and it carries things on top, so it's not an enclosed bag.
Types of bag.Envelope: An envelope is a paper holder that is more like a flat packet than a bag, and it's sealed with a flap.
Types of bag.Tin: A tin is a metal container, and the tin can for food was patented in 1810 before can openers were invented.
Types of bag.Egg carton: An egg carton is a molded tray, which has pockets for individual eggs and isn't a bag.
Types of bag.Shoebox: A shoebox is a rigid cardboard container, so it's a box rather than a bag, though it has plenty of other uses.

Things that have laces.Sneaker: Sneaker laces end in aglets, the little plastic tips, and the word 'sneaker' came from how quietly rubber soles let you creep.
Things that have laces.Hiking boot: Hiking boots use eyelets and hooks to get a tight fit, and a few special lacing knots can prevent blisters.
Things that have laces.Ice skate: Ice skates are laced tightly for ankle support, and skaters often lace the foot loosely and the ankle firmly for movement.
Things that have laces.Roller skate: Roller skates have laces, and early ones from the 1700s used wooden spools for wheels, before the modern quad skates.
Things that have laces.Oxford shoe: An Oxford shoe has closed lacing, and the eyelets are stitched under the vamp, unlike the open-laced 'Derby'.
Things that have laces.Football boot: Football boots have laces that are often covered by a flap, so the strings don't interfere with striking the ball.
Things that have laces.Baseball glove: A baseball glove has leather laces that bind the pieces together and that wear out and are replaced by pros every few seasons.
Things that have laces.American football: A football's laces give the quarterback a grip for spiraling the ball, and the laces are why it's easier to throw.
Things that have laces.Corset: A corset is laced at the back to cinch the waist, and in Victorian times, the waist could be reduced by several inches.
Things that have laces.Combat boot: Combat boots are laced up high to support the ankle, and many soldiers blouse their trousers inside to keep them tidy.
Things that have laces.Flip-flop: A flip-flop has a thong and no laces, which is the whole appeal of it for the beach.
Things that have laces.Loafer: A loafer is a slip-on shoe without laces, and the style came from a Norwegian fishermen's shoe in the 1930s.
Things that have laces.Slipper: A slipper slides on and off with no laces, which is why people wear them at home.
Things that have laces.Crocs: Crocs are foam clogs with holes and no laces, introduced in 2002 as a boat shoe.
Things that have laces.Wellington boot: A wellington is a pull-on rubber boot without laces, so it's easy to slip on and keep water out.
Things that have laces.Ballet flat: A ballet flat is a slip-on shoe, and it takes its design from the soft slippers of dancers, without laces.
Things that have laces.Mule: A mule is a backless shoe that slips on, and the name has been used for such shoes since at least the 1500s.
Things that have laces.Clog: A clog is a wooden or rubber shoe that you slip into, and the Dutch wooden clog is the best-known version.
Things that have laces.Necktie: A necktie is knotted but has no laces, and it's one of the few items to be said to have a knot instead.
Things that have laces.Belt: A belt is held with a buckle, so it has holes but no laces; a laced belt is a rare exception.
Things that have laces.Watch: A watch has a strap with a clasp, and a few straps with laces are rare, so it is basically a no.
Things that have laces.Sock: A sock is pulled on, and no laces are involved; it's the item that goes under the laced shoe.
Things that have laces.Mitten: A mitten covers the hand in one piece and has no laces, which is why a child can put it on easily.
Things that have laces.Baseball cap: A baseball cap has an adjustable strap, not laces, though the ball itself under the cap's bill is stitched.

Things used for mixing or stirring.Whisk: The whisk's wires trap air as they beat, which is how egg whites swell to several times their volume.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Hand mixer: Hand mixers took off after electric motors shrank enough in the 1920s to be held, turning minutes of beating into seconds.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Stand mixer: KitchenAid's famous stand mixer began as a commercial bakery machine and reached home kitchens in 1919.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Blender: Blenders mix by creating a vortex that pulls ingredients down onto the blades, which is why they struggle with very thick batters.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Food processor: A food processor chops and mixes with a flat S-blade. Carl Sontheimer popularized it in the US in the 1970s.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Wooden spoon: Wooden spoons don't conduct heat or scratch pots, and many cooks say they never need replacing.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Egg beater: The rotary egg beater used hand-cranked gears to spin two blades, an 1800s invention that predated electric mixers.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Cocktail shaker: Shaking in a shaker chills and dilutes a drink at once. That tiny melt of ice is part of the recipe.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Immersion blender: An immersion blender goes into the pot itself, so hot soup never has to be poured into a jug.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Milk frother: A milk frother whips air into milk to make foam. It works best with fresh milk that has plenty of protein.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Bread machine: Bread machines mix, knead, rise and bake in a single pan, and they became a home kitchen craze in the 1990s.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Grater: A grater shreds food into pieces. It scrapes rather than stirs, so it can't mix anything together.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Peeler: Peelers skim off a thin layer of skin. Swivel peelers pivot to follow a fruit's curves.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Corkscrew: A corkscrew's spiral bites into cork. It was patented in England in the 1600s, soon after wine corks became common.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Can opener: Can openers cut a lid from a tin. The tin can predates the can opener by about 40 years, so early cans were opened with chisels.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Tongs: Tongs grip and lift food but can't blend it. They are a lever, essentially two spoons joined at one end.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Colander: A colander drains pasta and veg. Its holes let water out while keeping food in, so nothing gets mixed.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Sieve: A sieve sifts flour and strains liquids. It separates fine from coarse instead of combining ingredients.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Rolling pin: Rolling pins flatten dough. French pins have no handles and taper at the ends, giving cooks finer control.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Cookie cutter: A cookie cutter stamps shapes from dough, and it can't mix a thing. Some come in elaborate holiday designs.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Pizza cutter: A pizza cutter is a rolling blade that slices through melted cheese without dragging toppings off.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Garlic press: A garlic press crushes cloves through small holes. It can taste harsher than chopping because it ruptures more cells.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Ice cream scoop: An ice cream scoop portions dessert. Its first patent dates to 1897, by Alfred Cralle, an African American inventor.
Things used for mixing or stirring.Toaster: A toaster browns bread with heated wires. It heats rather than mixes, and the Maillard reaction gives toast its flavor.

Things a scuba diver uses.Wetsuit: A wetsuit works by trapping a thin layer of water against the skin, which the body warms up.
Things a scuba diver uses.Fins: Fins let a diver move efficiently using the strong leg muscles, and they can multiply swimming power a lot.
Things a scuba diver uses.Dive mask: A mask traps a pocket of air in front of the eyes, because the human eye can't focus underwater.
Things a scuba diver uses.Regulator: The regulator reduces the high-pressure air from the tank to a pressure matching the water around the diver.
Things a scuba diver uses.Air tank: Most tanks have regular air, not pure oxygen, because breathing pure oxygen at depth can be toxic.
Things a scuba diver uses.Weight belt: Divers add lead weights because a wetsuit and the body float, and getting down means overcoming that.
Things a scuba diver uses.Dive computer: A dive computer tracks depth and time to warn when it's safe to rise, helping avoid decompression sickness.
Things a scuba diver uses.Depth gauge: A depth gauge matters because each 10 meters of seawater adds about one atmosphere of pressure.
Things a scuba diver uses.Buoyancy vest: A BCD inflates and deflates, and it lets divers float or hover, since neutral buoyancy is the key skill.
Things a scuba diver uses.Underwater torch: Water absorbs red light first, so at depth a torch restores the bright colors that disappear.
Things a scuba diver uses.Spacesuit: A spacesuit is for space, and while astronauts train underwater, the suit isn't a diving tool.
Things a scuba diver uses.Parachute: A parachute is for the sky, and a diver is going in the opposite direction.
Things a scuba diver uses.Ice axe: An ice axe is a mountaineer's tool, though ice divers go under frozen lakes using a different kind of gear.
Things a scuba diver uses.Crampons: Crampons are spikes for ice climbing and they'd be useless underwater.
Things a scuba diver uses.Skis: Skis are for snow and have nothing to do with diving.
Things a scuba diver uses.Snowshoes: Snowshoes keep one from sinking in snow, so the reverse of what a diver needs.
Things a scuba diver uses.Lunar rover: A rover drives on the Moon, which has no water, so a diver wouldn't use one.
Things a scuba diver uses.Saddle: A saddle is for horses, not for the seabed, although there are sea horses.
Things a scuba diver uses.Jetpack: Jetpacks are for air, and a diver uses fins and sometimes an underwater scooter.
Things a scuba diver uses.Hang glider: A hang glider rides air currents, and a diver is deep under in the water.
Things a scuba diver uses.Rollerblades: Rollerblades need a hard surface, so they would sink in the sea.
Things a scuba diver uses.Lasso: A lasso is for catching cattle, which don't live underwater.
Things a scuba diver uses.Climbing rope: Climbing rope is for cliffs and is something a diver would use only for a guideline, not for climbing.
Things a scuba diver uses.Ski poles: Ski poles are for balance on snow, and a diver glides with fins instead.

Japanese tech companies.Sony: Founded in 1946 as Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo, Sony gave the world the Walkman in 1979 and the PlayStation in 1994.
Japanese tech companies.Nintendo: The Kyoto firm began as a playing-card maker in 1889, long before Mario and the Switch.
Japanese tech companies.Panasonic: Founder Konosuke Matsushita started in 1918 making electric sockets; the company only took the Panasonic name worldwide in 2008.
Japanese tech companies.Toshiba: Toshiba made Japan's first electric light bulbs and early laptops, but it sold off its consumer PC business.
Japanese tech companies.Canon: Canon's name comes from Kwanon, a Buddhist goddess of mercy, and its first camera prototype used that name.
Japanese tech companies.Nikon: Nikon's lenses were made famous when war photographers discovered them in the Korean War, boosting its global reputation.
Japanese tech companies.Fujitsu: Fujitsu is one of Japan's oldest tech firms, founded in 1935, and once built the world's fastest supercomputer.
Japanese tech companies.Sharp: Sharp is named after its inventor's Ever-Sharp mechanical pencil, and it later made the first calculators using LCDs.
Japanese tech companies.Sega: The name is short for Service Games; Sega competed with Nintendo in the 1990s and now makes games only.
Japanese tech companies.Hitachi: Hitachi means 'rising sun' in the sense of Hitachi, the area in Ibaraki where its founder started the company in 1910.
Japanese tech companies.Casio: Casio launched the first all-electric compact calculator in 1957 and later made the famous G-Shock watch.
Japanese tech companies.NEC: NEC was founded in 1899 with American help and was once the world's largest PC maker in Japan.
Japanese tech companies.Epson: Epson's name means 'son of EP', for the small printer EP-101 it created in the 1960s for the Olympics.
Japanese tech companies.Samsung: Samsung is South Korean, so it looks Asian-Japanese-like but belongs to a different country.
Japanese tech companies.LG: LG is also South Korean; its name comes from the merger of Lucky and GoldStar.
Japanese tech companies.Huawei: Huawei is Chinese, founded in Shenzhen in 1987, and one of the biggest telecom equipment makers.
Japanese tech companies.Lenovo: Lenovo is Chinese-founded, in Beijing in 1984, even though it owns ThinkPad, which started at IBM.
Japanese tech companies.Nokia: Nokia is Finnish; it's a common guess, but its roots are in Finnish paper and rubber, not Japan.
Japanese tech companies.Philips: Philips is Dutch, founded in Eindhoven in 1891 initially making light bulbs, and it co-invented the compact disc with Sony.
Japanese tech companies.Siemens: Siemens is German, founded in Berlin in 1847, and began with telegraph equipment.
Japanese tech companies.Acer: Acer is Taiwanese and was founded in 1976 under the name Multitech.
Japanese tech companies.Asus: Asus is Taiwanese and takes its name from Pegasus, the winged horse, with the first letters dropped.
Japanese tech companies.Xiaomi: Xiaomi is Chinese, founded in Beijing in 2010, and its name is often translated as 'millet'.
Japanese tech companies.HTC: HTC is Taiwanese and built the first Android phone, the T-Mobile G1 in 2008.

Fonts.Arial: Created in 1982 by Monotype as a metric-compatible alternative to Helvetica for IBM printers.
Fonts.Helvetica: Designed in Switzerland in 1957, it is so widely used that it has its own feature-length documentary.
Fonts.Times New Roman: Designed in 1931 for the London newspaper The Times, which wanted a clearer, more economical typeface.
Fonts.Comic Sans: Designed in 1994 for the speech bubbles of Microsoft Bob's cartoon dog, and has been polarizing ever since.
Fonts.Calibri: Microsoft's Office default from 2007 until Aptos replaced it in 2023.
Fonts.Verdana: Designed by Matthew Carter in 1996 for screens, its name blends 'verdant' with Ana, a daughter of a Microsoft staffer.
Fonts.Courier: Typewriter-style and monospaced; the US State Department used it for decades before switching to Times New Roman in 2004.
Fonts.Garamond: Named after French punchcutter Claude Garamond, working in the 1500s; the Harry Potter books use a version of it.
Fonts.Futura: Paul Renner's 1927 design is the font on the plaque the Apollo 11 astronauts left on the Moon.
Fonts.Georgia: Designed by Matthew Carter in 1993 for the screen, and named after a tabloid headline 'Alien Heads Found in Georgia'.
Fonts.Impact: Created in 1965; it is the classic bold meme font, with white letters and a black outline.
Fonts.Papyrus: Designed in 1982 by Chris Costello, it's the font of the Avatar logo, and a 2017 SNL sketch mocked Ryan Gosling's obsession with it.
Fonts.Wingdings: A symbol font from 1990; a hoax claimed typing NYC in it gave a skull and Star of David, which fueled conspiracy rumors.
Fonts.Pixel: A pixel is the smallest unit of a picture, not a typeface.
Fonts.Serif: Serif describes letters with little feet, a style rather than a named font.
Fonts.Bold: Bold is a weight applied to a font, not a font itself.
Fonts.Italic: Italic style came from Venice around 1500, when Aldus Manutius used slanted type to save space.
Fonts.Kerning: Kerning adjusts spacing between letter pairs, a typographic technique and not a font.
Fonts.Pantone: Pantone is a color-matching system, not a font.
Fonts.Photoshop: Photoshop is image editing software, not a typeface.
Fonts.Canva: A design tool founded in 2013 in Australia, but not a font.
Fonts.Emoji: Japanese for picture and character; Shigetaka Kurita created the first set in 1999.
Fonts.Clipart: Clip art is ready-made illustrations, not a typeface.
Fonts.Bitmap: A bitmap is an image built from pixels, though early screens did use bitmap fonts.

Words typed using only the top keyboard.Typewriter: The classic trivia answer: all ten letters of 'typewriter' sit on the top row, so you can type it without moving your hands down.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Pretty: All six letters are on the top row. It comes from an Old English word meaning 'cunning', which gradually shifted to 'attractive'.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Pottery: A top-row word, and one of the oldest crafts: fired clay pots in Japan date back some 15,000 years or more.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Repertoire: At 10 letters, it's one of the longest English words typed using the top row alone, and it comes from the French for a 'list'.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Property: Another long top-row word, and it shares its root with 'proper', both coming from the Latin for 'one's own'.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Territory: All nine letters lie in the top row, and the word comes from a Latin word for the land around a town.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Quiet: A neat top-row word. Its Latin root means 'rest', and the term 'quietus' once meant a final release.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Route: All five letters are on the top row. It comes from the Latin for 'broken way', a path cut through a forest.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Write: Its silent W recalls a time when the letter was pronounced, as in Old English 'wrītan', which meant to scratch.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Puppy: A top-row word thanks to its Ps and Y. It comes from the French 'poupée' for doll, and puppies are born deaf.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Poetry: All six letters sit up top, and poetry predates writing, since the earliest epics were memorized and sung aloud.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Tower: Its five letters are all in the top row, and it comes from the Latin 'turris', the same root as 'turret'.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Twitter: Created in 2006, this top-row word was named after the short bursts of bird chatter. It was renamed X in 2023.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Keyboard: A trap: K, B, A and D force you down to the home and bottom rows, so you can't type it from the top row alone.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Computer: It needs M, C and others from the lower rows. Originally 'computer' meant a person who did calculations by hand.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Printer: Only the N dips to the bottom row, yet that's enough to fail. Gutenberg's press of the 1450s made printing a lasting trade.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Mouse: M and S lie off the top row. Its inventor, Douglas Engelbart, called it a mouse because the cord looked like a tail.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Quest: Q, U, E and T sit up top, but the S is on the home row, which rules it out. Quest comes from the Latin for 'seek'.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Water: W, A, T, E and R: the A is on the home row, which makes it a miss even though most letters are up top.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Tiger: T, I, E, R are up top, but G sits on the home row, so it misses. Every tiger's stripes are unique, like fingerprints.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Paper: A sits on the home row, so this near miss fails. Paper was invented in China, traditionally credited to Cai Lun around 105 CE.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Trumpet: T, R, U, P, E, T are all on the top row, but M is on the bottom row, which ruins it. Trumpets date back over 3,000 years.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Pirate: P, I, R, A, T, E: the A lives on the home row, so it breaks the pattern. The word comes from a Greek term for 'attacker'.
Words typed using only the top keyboard.Poster: Only the S sits off the top row, on the home row, so it just misses. The word first meant a post for notices.

Headphone and speaker brands.Bose: Founded in 1964 by MIT professor Amar Bose, it made its name with noise-cancelling headphones, first developed for pilots.
Headphone and speaker brands.Sennheiser: The German family firm began in 1945 and is known for open-back studio headphones, and its microphones are used in film production.
Headphone and speaker brands.Beats: Co-founded by Dr. Dre and Jimmy Iovine, it was bought by Apple in 2014 for about $3 billion, the company's biggest buy at the time.
Headphone and speaker brands.JBL: Named after founder James B. Lansing, the brand supplied loudspeakers to cinemas and concert halls long before portable speakers.
Headphone and speaker brands.Sony: Its Walkman, launched in 1979, made personal music portable and spawned a generation of headphone listening.
Headphone and speaker brands.Audio-Technica: Founded in Tokyo in 1962, it's loved by studios for affordable microphones and headphones, with the ATH-M50x a long-time favorite.
Headphone and speaker brands.Skullcandy: A Utah brand founded in 2003 by a snowboarder, it aimed headphones at skaters and snowboarders, with bold colors and graphics.
Headphone and speaker brands.Shure: Its SM58 microphone has been a stage standard since 1966, and its SM57 has been used for several US presidents' speeches.
Headphone and speaker brands.Bang & Olufsen: A Danish luxury brand founded in 1925, famous for sculptural designs, with some products displayed at New York's MoMA.
Headphone and speaker brands.Jabra: A Danish headset maker owned by GN, which grew from call-center headsets into popular wireless earbuds and conference speakers.
Headphone and speaker brands.Sonos: It pioneered multi-room wireless speakers in 2005, so music can fill the entire house from one app.
Headphone and speaker brands.Canon: Cameras and printers are Canon's business, not sound. It began as Kwanon, named after a Buddhist goddess of mercy.
Headphone and speaker brands.Nikon: Cameras and lenses are its craft, not audio, and Nikon cameras famously went into space on NASA missions.
Headphone and speaker brands.Nvidia: Its graphics chips drive games and AI, which makes it easy to confuse with gaming gear, but it sells no headphones or speakers.
Headphone and speaker brands.Intel: Best known for 'Intel Inside' stickers and processors, so it fits in a PC but doesn't make audio gear.
Headphone and speaker brands.Seagate: Hard drives are Seagate's trade, so it stores music rather than playing it through headphones or speakers.
Headphone and speaker brands.Netgear: Routers and switches are its field, so it connects your devices but doesn't make headphones or speakers.
Headphone and speaker brands.Adobe: Its Audition software edits sound, which makes it tempting, but Adobe builds software rather than headphones or speakers.
Headphone and speaker brands.Oracle: A database and cloud giant, so it manages data for banks, not music for your ears.
Headphone and speaker brands.Kodak: The film pioneer promised 'You press the button, we do the rest', a camera pitch rather than anything audio.
Headphone and speaker brands.GoPro: Rugged action cameras are its trademark, so it records video, but the company sells no speakers or headphones.
Headphone and speaker brands.Leica: This German camera maker, around since 1914, captures images rather than sound.
Headphone and speaker brands.Fujifilm: It's a photography and imaging brand, though it once sold blank audio cassettes, which is probably why it seems plausible.
Headphone and speaker brands.Pentax: A camera brand now under Ricoh, with decades of lenses behind it, and no speakers or headphones.

Fictional bears.Winnie-the-Pooh: The bear was named after Winnipeg, a real black bear from Canada who lived at London Zoo, and he's known for loving honey.
Fictional bears.Paddington: Michael Bond's marmalade-loving bear arrives from "darkest Peru" with a label saying "Please look after this bear".
Fictional bears.Baloo: The easygoing sloth bear teaches Mowgli the Law of the Jungle in Kipling's The Jungle Book, and sings "The Bare Necessities" in Disney's version.
Fictional bears.Rupert: The white-faced bear in checked trousers first appeared in the Daily Express in 1920, and his adventures have run for over a century.
Fictional bears.Corduroy: Don Freeman's 1968 toy bear loses a button in a department store and searches the store for it at night.
Fictional bears.Little Bear: Else Holmelund Minarik's gentle bear, illustrated by Maurice Sendak in 1957, plays pretend moon trips.
Fictional bears.Iorek Byrnison: The armoured polar bear in Philip Pullman's Northern Lights forges his own armour from meteoric iron and fights to regain his kingdom.
Fictional bears.Fozzie: The Muppets' stand-up comic bear, a hat-wearing performer, tells terrible jokes and says "Wocka wocka!"
Fictional bears.Yogi: The Hanna-Barbera bear, who is "smarter than the average bear", steals picnic baskets in Jellystone Park.
Fictional bears.Smokey: The US Forest Service mascot's famous slogan "Only you can prevent wildfires" dates from 1944, and a real rescued cub was named Smokey in 1950.
Fictional bears.Tigger: Pooh's bouncy friend is a tiger, not a bear, as he has told everyone repeatedly.
Fictional bears.Eeyore: The gloomy donkey is Pooh's friend, but he's a donkey.
Fictional bears.Mowgli: Kipling's wolf-raised boy is the man-cub who befriends Baloo, a human, not a bear.
Fictional bears.Bagheera: Mowgli's panther mentor in The Jungle Book is a black leopard, a big cat, and so not a bear like Baloo.
Fictional bears.Shere Khan: The tiger villain of The Jungle Book fears fire and is a cat, not a bear.
Fictional bears.Aslan: C. S. Lewis's Narnian king is a lion and a Christ-like figure.
Fictional bears.Simba: The lion cub from The Lion King is a cat, and his name means "lion" in Swahili.
Fictional bears.Babar: Jean de Brunhoff's elephant king is no bear.
Fictional bears.Kanga: The mother kangaroo of the Hundred Acre Wood is a marsupial.
Fictional bears.Hobbes: Calvin's stuffed tiger in Bill Watterson's comic is a tiger, not a bear.
Fictional bears.Garfield: Jim Davis's orange cat is a cat, not a bear.
Fictional bears.Clifford: Norman Bridwell's giant red dog is a dog, not a bear.
Fictional bears.Mr. Toad: The boastful toad of Toad Hall is an amphibian.
Fictional bears.Tony the Tiger: Kellogg's Frosted Flakes mascot, a tiger, says "They're Gr-r-reat!"

Things with a spiral or coil shape.Snail shell: Most snail shells spiral in one direction, clockwise, and a rare snail with a reversed, left-coiling shell is a collector's prize.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Corkscrew: The helical worm of a corkscrew bores into the cork, and the first patent for one was granted in England in 1795 to Samuel Henshall.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Slinky: The Slinky was invented in 1943 by a naval engineer, Richard James, who saw a torsion spring fall off a shelf and walk.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.DNA: DNA is a double helix with about ten base pairs per turn, and the structure was announced by Watson and Crick in 1953.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Spiral staircase: The tight spiral saves floor space, and in many medieval castles it turned clockwise going up, which is said to favor defenders swinging right-handed.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Milky Way: Our galaxy is a barred spiral, with the Sun sitting in a minor arm, about 26,000 light years from the galactic center.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Fiddlehead fern: The curled-up new frond of a fern is edible in spring, and its spiral is named after the scroll of a violin.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Cinnamon roll: Swedish kanelbullar are famous cinnamon swirls, and Sweden even celebrates a Cinnamon Bun Day every October 4th.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Nautilus shell: Its chambered shell grows in a logarithmic spiral, and the animal inside adds a new chamber as it grows.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Ram's horn: A ram's horn spirals as it grows, never being shed, and the Jewish shofar is made from one.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Drill bit: A twist drill has spiral grooves that carry shavings out of the hole as it bores, and Stephen Morse patented it in the 1860s.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Fusilli: The pasta's corkscrew shape traps sauce in its grooves, and its name is related to Italian for spindle, fuso.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Coil spring: Coil springs store energy when compressed, and many car suspensions use them to soak up bumps.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Penne: Penne is a straight tube cut diagonally into points at both ends, and its name comes from Italian for pen quills.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Ruler: A ruler is a flat straight strip, and its name comes from the way it rules straight lines on paper.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Pencil: A pencil's 'lead' is graphite mixed with clay, named after lead because graphite once got mistaken for a lead ore, and it's a straight hexagonal rod.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Brick: A brick is a straight-edged block, a shape with no curl at all, and one that the ancient Mesopotamians already baked.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Baseball bat: A bat is a straight, tapered cylinder, usually made of ash, maple or birch, in the major leagues.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Ladder: A ladder is a pair of straight rails joined by rungs, which is flat, unlike a spiral staircase.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Spaghetti: A strand of spaghetti is straight, and its name is Italian for little strings, though twirling it on a fork makes a coil.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Banana: A banana is curved in a single arc rather than coiled, and it is technically a berry.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Domino: A domino is a flat rectangle, twice as long as wide, and its pips are the same dots as on dice.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Chopstick: A chopstick is a straight stick, and the pair originated in China more than 3,000 years ago.
Things with a spiral or coil shape.Crayon: A crayon is a straight, round stick of wax, and the name comes from the French craie, meaning chalk.

Things associated with Halloween.Jack-o'-lantern: The tradition started in Ireland with carved turnips and potatoes. Immigrants to America found pumpkins were bigger and far easier to carve.
Things associated with Halloween.Trick-or-treat: Children going door to door grew from medieval 'souling', when the poor sang prayers for the dead in return for soul cakes.
Things associated with Halloween.Costume: People once wore disguises on Halloween to avoid being recognized by wandering spirits. The Celtic festival Samhain began the custom.
Things associated with Halloween.Cauldron: A cauldron is a big pot hung over a fire. Witches stirring brews in them became a staple image partly thanks to Shakespeare's Macbeth.
Things associated with Halloween.Broomstick: Witches riding brooms may trace to medieval accusations of using flying ointments applied with a broomstick. Brooms were also a women's household tool.
Things associated with Halloween.Cobweb: Spider silk is, weight for weight, tougher than steel. Fake stretchy cobwebs are a cheap way to make any room look abandoned.
Things associated with Halloween.Skeleton: An adult human has 206 bones, but babies are born with around 300 that fuse together as they grow.
Things associated with Halloween.Bat: Bats are the only mammals that truly fly. Their link to Halloween comes from nocturnal habits and caves, plus vampire legends.
Things associated with Halloween.Ghost: Ghost stories fit Halloween because the Celts believed the boundary between living and dead thinned on Samhain night, October 31.
Things associated with Halloween.Candy corn: Developed in the 1880s, its three-color stripes mimic a corn kernel, a fitting treat for farming America. Today it is sold mostly around Halloween.
Things associated with Halloween.Witch: Witches became Halloween icons partly because Samhain was a time of spells and divination. Witch trials of the 1600s added darker imagery.
Things associated with Halloween.Mummy: Egyptians removed organs and dried bodies with natron salt, a process taking about 70 days. Victorian unwrapping parties later made mummies spooky.
Things associated with Halloween.Black cat: Black cats were once linked to witches' familiars, but in ancient Egypt they were revered. Some shelters now limit adoptions around Halloween.
Things associated with Halloween.Haunted house: Haunted houses go back to stories of restless spirits, but the walk-through attraction took off in America in the 1970s.
Things associated with Halloween.Mistletoe: Mistletoe is a Christmas plant, a kissing tradition at winter parties. It does not belong to Halloween.
Things associated with Halloween.Egg hunt: Egg hunts belong to Easter, when children search gardens for hidden decorated or chocolate eggs.
Things associated with Halloween.Tinsel: Shiny strands of metallic foil are for Christmas trees, not Halloween. They were originally made from real silver.
Things associated with Halloween.Shamrock: The shamrock is Ireland's emblem for St. Patrick's Day on March 17, not for Halloween despite Halloween's Irish roots.
Things associated with Halloween.Maypole: A maypole is danced around on May 1, celebrating spring. It's a different seasonal festival from October's Halloween.
Things associated with Halloween.Menorah: The Hanukkah menorah holds candles lit across eight nights in December, a Jewish festival of lights with no role in Halloween.
Things associated with Halloween.Cupid: Cupid is the cherub of Valentine's Day, firing arrows of love. Halloween leans toward ghosts, not romance.
Things associated with Halloween.Sleigh: Santa's sleigh is a Christmas image. Sleighs are snow vehicles pulled by horses or reindeer, not a Halloween item.
Things associated with Halloween.Easter bonnet: The decorated hat is part of Easter parades, a spring celebration, rather than an autumn one.
Things associated with Halloween.Reindeer: Reindeer pull Santa's sleigh at Christmas. They are one of the few deer species where both sexes grow antlers.

Folklore figures who bring gifts.Santa Claus: The American Santa grew from Dutch Sinterklaas. Coca-Cola's 1930s ads popularized the red suit, though he was already often shown in red.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Tooth Fairy: A modern tradition, mostly from early 1900s America. Spanish-speaking children often get a visit from Ratoncito Perez, a mouse.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Easter Bunny: Brought by German immigrants, who told of the Osterhase, a hare that left eggs for good children.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.La Befana: The kindly Italian witch who delivers gifts on the eve of Epiphany, sweeping the house as she goes.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Sinterklaas: Dutch children set out shoes for him with a carrot for his horse. He arrives from Spain by steamboat in mid-November.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Father Christmas: The British figure was once about feasting and cheer, not gifts. He merged with Santa in the Victorian era.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Ded Moroz: Russia's Grandfather Frost arrives at New Year, often with his granddaughter Snegurochka, rather than on Christmas.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Christkind: In German-speaking lands, the gift bringer is an angelic child. Martin Luther is often credited with promoting this to replace Saint Nicholas.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Saint Nicholas: A 4th-century bishop of Myra, in present-day Turkey, known for secret gift-giving, including dowries for poor girls.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Krampus: The Alpine devil who punishes bad children, often at the side of Saint Nicholas, and carries chains.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Grinch: Dr. Seuss's 1957 character tries to steal Christmas gifts, rather than deliver them. A trap, since he ends up giving.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Jack Frost: A winter spirit who nips noses and paints frost on windows. He brings cold, not gifts.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Cupid: The Roman love god shoots arrows at hearts rather than bringing presents.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Boogeyman: A made-up monster invoked to scare children into behaving, the opposite of a gift giver.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Headless Horseman: Washington Irving's ghost who hunts Ichabod Crane with a pumpkin. He brings fright, not gifts.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Bloody Mary: Said to appear in mirrors when her name is chanted in a dark room. A scary game, not a gift giver.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Rumpelstiltskin: The imp who spins straw into gold, but wants a firstborn child as payment, so he's no gift giver.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Mother Nature: A personification of the natural world. She doesn't deliver presents.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Father Time: An old man with a scythe and hourglass who marks the passing year, not a giver of presents.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Old Man Winter: A personification of the cold season, who nips at noses and blows cold winds, not a bringer of gifts.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Punxsutawney Phil: The Pennsylvania groundhog has predicted weather every Groundhog Day since 1887, but he leaves no gifts.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Bigfoot: The legendary ape-like creature of the Pacific Northwest, made famous by a 1967 film. He leaves only footprints.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Medusa: The Greek Gorgon with snakes for hair brings stone statues, not gifts.
Folklore figures who bring gifts.Baba Yaga: The Slavic witch who lives in a hut on chicken legs. She sometimes helps, but also sometimes eats people.

Prey of polar bears.Ringed seal: The polar bear's main prey; bears wait at breathing holes in the ice or smash into the snow lairs where pups are hidden.
Prey of polar bears.Bearded seal: A big Arctic seal with long whiskers; polar bears take them, especially young ones, on the sea ice.
Prey of polar bears.Harp seal: Harp seals gather in huge breeding herds on ice in late winter, offering bears in that region a rich seasonal meal.
Prey of polar bears.Hooded seal: Males inflate a red nasal balloon when threatened or courting; polar bears hunt them on the ice around Greenland.
Prey of polar bears.Beluga: Bears sometimes ambush belugas trapped by ice at small breathing holes; the whale's pale skin blends with the ice.
Prey of polar bears.Narwhal: The 'unicorn of the sea' can get trapped by ice, giving polar bears a chance; its tusk is actually a long tooth.
Prey of polar bears.Walrus: Walruses can weigh over a tonne, so bears usually target the young or weak rather than risk the tusks.
Prey of polar bears.Seabird eggs: When summer ice melts and seals are out of reach, hungry bears raid cliffs and nests for eggs.
Prey of polar bears.Whale carcass: Bears scavenge beached whales, and several often feed together without fighting, which is unusual for solitary hunters.
Prey of polar bears.Seal pups: Newborn ringed seals hide in snow lairs, but a polar bear can smell them through the snow and crash through the roof.
Prey of polar bears.Penguin: Penguins live in the Southern Hemisphere and polar bears in the Arctic, so the two never meet in the wild.
Prey of polar bears.Emperor penguin: Lives only around Antarctica, at the opposite end of the Earth from polar bears.
Prey of polar bears.Leopard seal: A fierce Antarctic predator that hunts penguins, living on the opposite side of the planet from polar bears.
Prey of polar bears.Weddell seal: This Antarctic seal can dive deep for over an hour and stays beneath ice; polar bears never meet it.
Prey of polar bears.Krill: Tiny shrimp-like crustaceans central to Antarctic food webs; polar bears don't eat them, though many seals and whales do.
Prey of polar bears.Crabeater seal: Despite the name, it eats krill rather than crabs, and it lives around Antarctica, far from polar bears.
Prey of polar bears.Sea lion: Sea lions mostly live on temperate coasts; they differ from true seals by having visible ear flaps.
Prey of polar bears.Albatross: Wandering albatrosses have wingspans up to about 3.5 meters and ride Southern Ocean winds, far from the Arctic.
Prey of polar bears.Kangaroo: A marsupial of Australia; a polar bear would never meet one outside a zoo.
Prey of polar bears.Zebra: An African grassland animal with no connection to Arctic ice and snow.
Prey of polar bears.Bison: Bison roam the plains and forests of North America, far from the Arctic sea ice where polar bears hunt.
Prey of polar bears.Elephant seal: A huge seal of the Southern Ocean whose males can weigh several tonnes; polar bears never hunt it.
Prey of polar bears.Ross seal: A rarely seen Antarctic pack-ice seal that makes odd trilling calls, far from polar bear territory.
Prey of polar bears.Adelie penguin: Named by explorer Dumont d'Urville after his wife Adele; it lives only in Antarctica, not where polar bears roam.

Real pirates (not fictional ones).Blackbeard: Edward Teach reportedly lit slow-burning fuses under his hat to look demonic; he was killed in 1718 off North Carolina.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Anne Bonny: This Irish-born pirate sailed with Calico Jack and was spared the gallows after claiming to be pregnant.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Mary Read: She lived disguised as a man for years, fought as a soldier, then turned pirate; she died in a Jamaican prison around 1721.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Calico Jack: John Rackham got his nickname from his colorful clothes, and is popularly credited with the skull-and-crossed-swords flag.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Captain Kidd: William Kidd was hanged in London in 1701, and his rumored buried treasure fed centuries of treasure-hunting legends.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Black Bart: Bartholomew Roberts captured over 400 ships in a few years, probably more than any other pirate in history.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Stede Bonnet: The 'Gentleman Pirate' was a wealthy Barbados landowner with no sailing experience who bought his own ship and turned pirate.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Ching Shih: She led a fleet of hundreds of ships in early 1800s China, then took a government pardon and retired rich, rare for a pirate.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Barbarossa: Hayreddin 'Red Beard' rose from Ottoman corsair to admiral of the Ottoman fleet in the 1500s.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Black Sam Bellamy: His ship Whydah sank in a 1717 storm off Cape Cod; the wreck, found in 1984, is the first authenticated pirate ship ever discovered.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Edward Low: Notorious for cruelty even among pirates, he vanished around 1724 and his fate remains uncertain.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Henry Every: His 1695 capture of the Mughal treasure ship Ganj-i-Sawai made him the most wanted man alive; he then vanished with the loot.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Captain Hook: J. M. Barrie's villain is fictional, and in the book he is a snob who went to Eton, a gentleman among pirates.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Long John Silver: Robert Louis Stevenson invented him for Treasure Island in 1883; the parrot on the shoulder trope traces largely to him.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Jack Sparrow: A fictional hero of Pirates of the Caribbean; Johnny Depp has said he drew on rock guitarist Keith Richards.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Davy Jones: A folklore sailors' devil of the sea, not a person: 'Davy Jones' locker' means the ocean floor.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Captain Flint: In Treasure Island, Flint is already dead when the story opens; Long John Silver's parrot is named after him.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Captain Pugwash: A British children's cartoon pirate; a rumor of rude crew names was a hoax, and creator John Ryan won a libel case over it.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Barbossa: The Pirates of the Caribbean villain's name echoes the real corsair Barbarossa, but the character is invented.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Dread Pirate Roberts: In The Princess Bride the title is passed from one man to the next, so this fearsome pirate is a recycled fiction.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Captain Blood: Hero of Rafael Sabatini's 1922 novel, a doctor turned pirate; the 1935 film made Errol Flynn a star.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Guybrush Threepwood: The hero of the Monkey Island games, a would-be pirate who boasts he can hold his breath for ten minutes.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).One-Eyed Willy: The ghost pirate of The Goonies (1985) guards a booby-trapped hoard; the character was invented for the film.
Real pirates (not fictional ones).Monkey D. Luffy: The rubber-bodied hero of the manga One Piece, one of the best-selling manga ever, with hundreds of millions of copies sold.

Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Kanelbulle: Swedish cinnamon buns have their own national day, on 4 October.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Köttbullar: Swedish meatballs went global through IKEA; Sweden once tweeted that King Charles XII likely brought the recipe from Ottoman Turkey.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Gravlax: Salmon cured with salt, sugar and dill; the name means 'buried salmon', since it was originally buried in the ground.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Surströmming: Fermented Baltic herring whose smell is so strong that cans are famously opened outdoors, and some airlines ban it.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Princess cake: A green marzipan dome of cake and cream, called prinsesstarta, said to be named for the princesses its inventor taught.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Knäckebröd: Crisp rye crispbread, a Swedish staple for centuries; the traditional hole let loaves hang from poles to dry.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Kladdkaka: The name means 'sticky cake': a gooey chocolate cake whose underbaked, fudgy middle is intentional.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Semla: A cardamom bun with almond paste and cream; King Adolf Frederick reportedly died in 1771 after eating 14 of them.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Smörgåsbord: Swedish for 'sandwich table', it gave English the word for a lavish buffet spread.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Janssons frestelse: 'Jansson's temptation': potato, onion and sprats baked in cream, a Christmas table standard.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Lussekatter: Saffron buns baked for St. Lucia's Day on 13 December, shaped like curled 'S' forms.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Prinskorv: Small 'prince sausages', a staple of the Swedish Christmas smorgasbord and children's parties.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Smørrebrød: Denmark's open-faced sandwiches on rye, named from Danish for 'butter bread', so not Swedish.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Fårikål: Norway's national dish of lamb and cabbage, with its own feast day in late September.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Brunost: Norwegian brown cheese, made by caramelizing whey into a sweet, fudgy slice.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Karjalanpiirakka: Finnish Karelian pies, ryebread shells with rice filling, are an EU-protected traditional food, so Finnish rather than Swedish.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Frikadeller: Danish pan-fried meatballs, a cousin of the Swedish ones but definitely Danish.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Flæskesteg: Danish roast pork with crackling, a Christmas dinner centerpiece in Denmark.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Kransekake: A tower of almond rings served at Norwegian weddings and celebrations, so Norwegian (and Danish), not Swedish.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Pinnekjøtt: A Norwegian Christmas dish of salted lamb ribs steamed over birch twigs.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Aebleskiver: Danish round pancake balls cooked in a special pan and eaten at Christmas.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Wienerbrød: Danish pastry, whose name means 'Vienna bread', after Austrian bakers who popularized it there.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Lefse: A soft Norwegian flatbread made with potatoes, much loved in Norwegian-American communities.
Swedish foods (not Danish or Norwegian).Salmiakki: Finnish salty licorice flavored with ammonium chloride, an acquired taste so Finnish, not Swedish.
